<u>Social impacts</u>: The endangered species program will result in noneconomic impacts that will be felt only by people.
Wild animal populations can serve as carriers or vectors of diseases and parasites that are harmful to humans. Although serious epidemics or outbreaks of such diseases are more characteristic of higher density wildlife populations that are not endangered, endangered animals may on occasion be involved. Protection of endangered populations that might become carriers would probably mean more careful use of population reduction against the host species. There may be a slightly greater risk to humans when control of the disease involves an endangered species because a reduction of an endangered population would be more carefully considered before implementation. Bats, as a group, are known to be carriers of rabies. If a population of Indiana bats was believed to be involved in a rabies outbreak threatening humans, there would be a greater effort to establish that fact and consider all alternatives before outright reduction of the endangered Indiana bat population was employed. Prairie dogs are known to carry sylvatic plague to which humans are susceptible. Certainly routine reduction of the endangered Utah prairie dog population would be avoided on the basis of that fact alone. The result would be slightly higher risk to humans where endangered animals are the vectors involved.
